sections.title: Not knowing
sections.blurb: Kinds of not knowing, and who has to show what before a step.

terms.definition: Not knowing what will happen, while knowing the odds.
terms.note: A fair die. Outside textbooks, almost nothing is pure risk.

terms.definition: Not knowing the odds either, and perhaps no one can.
terms.note: Knight and Keynes, 1921. Keynes, in 1937: "We simply do not know." Bayesians answer that you can always put a number on a belief; the dispute is how far to trust it.

terms.definition: Knowing a chance is there without knowing its size: an urn whose mix you are not told.
terms.note: Ellsberg, 1961. Many people steer away from it; whether that is wise is disputed.

terms.definition: Giving each answer equal odds because you know nothing that favours one.
terms.note: Keynes named it in 1921 and showed its trap: cut the question another way and the equal odds change. A coin flipped at a question you know nothing about uses it.

terms.definition: How common something is before you look at the details of this case.
terms.note: Skip it, and one positive test makes a rare thing look likely.

terms.definition: A chance given something: the chance of rain, given dark clouds.
terms.note: Many would say every probability is given something; the condition is often left unsaid.

terms.definition: The group of past cases a new case is counted among.
terms.note: Count it in another group and you get another honest number. For a new kind of thing there may be no group to count.

terms.definition: Open to being shown wrong: some possible observation could refute it.
terms.note: Popper's test. A claim can be falsifiable in principle and still untestable in time: if the first real test is the step itself, "it will be safe" is checked only by taking it.

terms.definition: Who has to convince whom, and which side wins while the evidence is unclear.
terms.note: The tree's gate: for a step that cannot be undone or tried first, whoever takes it has to show it is safe.

terms.definition: Acting against a serious or irreversible harm before it is proven.
terms.note: Weak form: Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 15, where lack of certainty is no reason to wait. Strong form: the Wingspread Statement, 1998, which puts the burden of proof on whoever takes the step. Critics answer that stopping has risks too.

terms.definition: An outcome with no way back, so there is no next try to learn from.
terms.note: An average over many tries says little when one try can end the game.
